verses.text: All the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in the place of his father Amaziah.
He built Eloth, and restored it to Judah, after that the king slept with his fathers.
Uzziah was sixteen years old when he began to reign; and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jechiliah, of Jerusalem.
He did that which was right in Yahweh’s eyes, according to all that his father Amaziah had done.
He set himself to seek God in the days of Zechariah, who had understanding in the vision of God; and as long as he sought Yahweh, God made him prosper.
He went out and fought against the Philistines, and broke down the wall of Gath, the wall of Jabneh, and the wall of Ashdod; and he built cities in the country of Ashdod, and among the Philistines.
God helped him against the Philistines, and against the Arabians who lived in Gur Baal, and the Meunim.
The Ammonites gave tribute to Uzziah. His name spread abroad even to the entrance of Egypt; for he grew exceedingly strong.
Moreover Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the corner gate, at the valley gate, and at the turning of the wall, and fortified them.

He built towers in the wilderness, and dug out many cisterns, for he had much livestock; in the lowland also, and in the plain. He had farmers and vineyard keepers in the mountains and in the fruitful fields, for he loved farming.

Moreover Uzziah had an army of fighting men, who went out to war by bands, according to the number of their reckoning made by Jeiel the scribe and Maaseiah the officer, under the hand of Hananiah, one of the king’s captains.
The whole number of the heads of fathers’ households, even the mighty men of valor, was two thousand six hundred.
Under their hand was an army, three hundred seven thousand five hundred, who made war with mighty power, to help the king against the enemy.
Uzziah prepared for them, even for all the army, shields, spears, helmets, coats of mail, bows, and stones for slinging.

In Jerusalem, he made devices, invented by skillful men, to be on the towers and on the battlements, with which to shoot arrows and great stones. His name spread far abroad, because he was marvelously helped until he was strong.
But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up, so that he did corruptly, and he trespassed against Yahweh his God; for he went into Yahweh’s temple to burn incense on the altar of incense.
Azariah the priest went in after him, and with him eighty priests of Yahweh, who were valiant men.

They resisted Uzziah the king, and said to him, “It isn’t for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to Yahweh, but for the priests the sons of Aaron, who are consecrated to burn incense. Go out of the sanctuary, for you have trespassed. It will not be for your honor from Yahweh God.”

Then Uzziah was angry. He had a censer in his hand to burn incense, and while he was angry with the priests, the leprosy broke out on his forehead before the priests in Yahweh’s house, beside the altar of incense.

Azariah the chief priest, and all the priests, looked at him, and behold, he was leprous in his forehead, and they thrust him out quickly from there. Yes, he himself also hurried to go out, because Yahweh had struck him.

Uzziah the king was a leper to the day of his death, and lived in a separate house, being a leper; for he was cut off from Yahweh’s house. Jotham his son was over the king’s house, judging the people of the land.
Now the rest of the acts of Uzziah, first and last, Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, wrote.
So Uzziah slept with his fathers; and they buried him with his fathers in the field of burial which belonged to the kings, for they said, “He is a leper.” Jotham his son reigned in his place.

footnotes.content: Young Uzziah steps into his father's throne at sixteen — so much ambition, so much life ahead. I've learned that the Lord's favor comes not to those who seize a throne by strength, but to those who receive their calling with a humble heart and ask Him to guide each step.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eloth, a port city, restored to Judah — a small act of recovery after his father's loss. Even in youth, Uzziah does practical work, rebuilding what was broken. The Lord often honors such earnestness, even before we know how far we'll fall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sixteen when he began to reign, fifty-two years in Jerusalem — a full life of power granted by the Lord. His mother Jechiliah stood behind him. How much of our steadiness comes from those who raised us? I think the Lord sees that too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He did what was right because his father Amaziah showed him the way. Obedience to what's true flows downward, parent to child, if the heart is watching. This is the foundation — before fortune, before power, a life built on righteousness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zechariah, a prophet with understanding in God's vision, mentored him. "As long as he sought Yahweh, God made him prosper" — that little word 'as long' carries all the weight of this story. Seeking the Lord is what unlocks blessing; losing that seeking is what locks us out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gath, Jabneh, Ashdod — the names of Philistine strongholds, broken by Uzziah's hand. Military victories, gained by God's power working through a young king willing to fight for his people. Yet victories can breed the very pride that undoes us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "God helped him" — three words that frame everything. The Arabians of Gur Baal, the Meunim — none of them stand against a king whom God strengthens. I pray we remember, in our own small battles, that all good coming is His hand extended.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His name reaches even to Egypt — fame spreading like a shadow cast by God's favor. The Ammonites bow. Uzziah grows exceedingly strong. The trap is set, though he doesn't see it yet. Strength without humility is a stage for a fall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Corner gate, valley gate, walls fortified — Uzziah builds and strengthens Jerusalem. These are real acts of stewardship, caring for the city God gave him. Yet brick and mortar can deceive us into thinking we are the builders when we are only servants.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Towers, cisterns, farms, vineyards — Uzziah is a man of practical vision, making the land fruitful. "He loved farming" — that touch reveals him: not a tyrant, but a builder who knows the earth. Good work in itself, yet all his cleverness cannot buy him humility.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeiel the scribe, Maaseiah the officer, Hananiah the captain — good men serving under him, keeping careful count of the army's strength. They see the numbers, the order, the power growing. But none can see the pride that grows unseen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twenty-six hundred mighty men of valor, heads of families. Each one a warrior, each one part of the machinery of power. They are Uzziah's pride made flesh — the proof of his strength, which is also the proof of his danger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three hundred and seven thousand five hundred — the number is staggering, almost numbing. Such an army could take almost any city. When numbers grow this large, we start to forget that every soldier is a soul, and God sees each one. The king is beginning to see only his own reflection in the mirror of his might.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shields, spears, helmets, mail, bows, stones for slinging — every tool of war is ready and waiting. Uzziah is a skilled quartermaster, thinking of his army's needs. Yet preparation for war is not the same as preparation of the heart. A well-armed soldier with a proud king will still break like pottery.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ingenious war machines, invented by skillful men, shoot arrows and stones from high places. Uzziah's engineers earn their fame by his favor, but listen: "His name spread far abroad, because he was marvelously helped until he was strong." That word 'until' is a hinge. God's help had a door.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up." The hinge turns. Pride enters like leprosy entering the skin — invisible at first, a whisper that he deserves more, that he has earned a privilege not given to other men. He walks into God's temple to burn incense, a priest's sacred work, and in that moment the rebellion is complete.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Azariah and eighty priests, valiant men, follow Uzziah into the temple. They are watching, listening. Do they see the danger already in his eyes? The Lord sends faithful witnesses even as sin moves in.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "It isn't for you" — the priest's words are clear and low. Only the sons of Aaron, set apart, can burn incense. The boundary is drawn by the Lord Himself, not by accident or tradition. Azariah speaks with the gentleness of a warning: "It will not be for your honor from Yahweh God." Even now, a door left open to repent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Uzziah is angry — rage at being told no, rage at a boundary drawn by God Himself. The censer is in his hand, his pride ablaze. And in that moment of defiance, the leprosy breaks out on his forehead, visible to all. The Lord speaks not in words, but in flesh. Judgment is written on him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priests look, and what they see is the living judgment of God — leprosy spreading on the king's forehead. They push him out quickly; he rushes to leave himself, understanding in that instant what his pride has cost him. Sometimes the Lord speaks in a way that cannot be misunderstood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Uzziah lives to the end of his days cut off from the Lord's house, separated by disease and by God's decree. His son Jotham takes the throne. Readers today hear an echo: how many good beginnings are undone by the hour we forget whose kingdom this is, and begin to think it is ours. The Lord is jealous for His own holiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaiah the prophet writes down Uzziah's story — "the rest of the acts, first and last." Isaiah, the great prophet, records both the rise and the fall. The Lord preserves the whole account so we might learn from it: pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Uzziah sleeps with his fathers but is buried apart, in a separate field, marked 'He is a leper.' Even in death, the boundary holds. His son Jotham inherits his throne, but not his disgrace. The Lord's judgment is stern because His love is complete; He does not let us pretend pride is nothing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
